items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use Cartesian coordinates to define vectors in the plane. For example, consider the diagram shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e97a6041545df91681d9e8016680f7e6]

Content:
The point [MATH: A] has coordinates [MATH: (2,3).] We also have the point [MATH: O(0,0)] that is called the origin.

Content:
The vector [MATH: \overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}] is called the position vector of [MATH: A.] A position vector always has its tail at the origin.

Content:
Now let's define two special unit vectors [MATH: \mathbf{i}] and [MATH: \mathbf{j},] where [MATH: |\, \mathbf{i} \,| = |\, \mathbf{j} \,| = 1,] as follows:

Content:
- [MATH: \mathbf{i}] is a horizontal unit vector that points to the right along the positive direction of the [MATH: x]-axis, while
- [MATH: \mathbf{j}] is a vertical unit vector that points upwards along the positive direction of the [MATH: y]-axis.

Content:
These vectors are shown in the picture below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/defd246768f6d14327096ba9d487ee28]

Content:
We have

Content:
[MATH: OX^(→) = 2i,; XA^(→) = OY^(→) = 3j.]

Content:
Now, from [MATH: \triangle OXA,] we have

Content:
[MATH: OA^(→)|= OX^(→) + XA^(→); = 2i + 3j.]

Content:
So, the point [MATH: A] with coordinates [MATH: (2,3)] has a position vector
[MATH: OA^(→)|= 2i + 3j.]

Content:
In general, if a point [MATH: A] has coordinates [MATH: (a_x,a_y),] then its position vector is given by

Content:
[MATH: \overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a} = a_x\mathbf{i}+a_y\mathbf{j}.]

Content:
The [MATH: \mathbf{i,j}] notation can sometimes be cumbersome. An alternative is to use angle bracket notation. For example, using angle bracket notation, the vector [MATH: 2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}] can be expressed as

Content:
[MATH: 2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}=\langle 2,3 \rangle.]

Content:
Note that, using angle bracket notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as
[MATH: i = 1i + 0j = ⟨1, 0⟩,; j = 0i + 1j = ⟨0, 1⟩.]

Content:
We can also use column vector notation, which is similar to angle bracket notation but expresses the vector as a column rather than a row. For example, using column vector notation, the vector [MATH: 2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}] can be expressed as

Content:
[MATH: [2; 3]]

Content:
Using column vector notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as [MATH: [1; 0]] and [MATH: [0; 1]]

Content:
Note: Sometimes, the round bracket notation [MATH: (\ldots)] is used to denote vectors. However, we will avoid using that notation here, because it also looks like the coordinates of a point. A point and its position vector are two separate objects!

Item 5 — Tutorial: Alternatives to i,j Notation

Content:
The [MATH: \mathbf{i,j}] notation can sometimes be cumbersome. An alternative is to use angle bracket notation. For example, using angle bracket notation, the vector [MATH: 2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}] can be expressed as

Content:
[MATH: 2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}=\langle 2,3 \rangle.]

Content:
Note that, using angle bracket notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as
[MATH: i = 1i + 0j = ⟨1, 0⟩,; j = 0i + 1j = ⟨0, 1⟩.]

Content:
We can also use column vector notation, which is similar to angle bracket notation but expresses the vector as a column rather than a row. For example, using column vector notation, the vector [MATH: 2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}] can be expressed as

Content:
[MATH: [2; 3]]

Content:
Using column vector notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as [MATH: [1; 0]] and [MATH: [0; 1]]

Content:
Note: Sometimes, the round bracket notation [MATH: (\ldots)] is used to denote vectors. However, we will avoid using that notation here, because it also looks like the coordinates of a point. A point and its position vector are two separate objects!

Item 9 — Example: Expressing a Vector in Component Form

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: A(-2,1)] and [MATH: B(2,3).] Find [MATH: \overrightarrow{AB}] in terms of [MATH: \mathbf{i}] and [MATH: \mathbf{j}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Our vector is shown in the diagram below.

[IMG: /graphics/953fe3c079f7beda77cf172d63fccd10]

We have

[MATH: OA^(→) = a = − 2i + j,; OB^(→) = b = 2i + 3j.]

Now, from [MATH: \triangle OAB,] we have

[MATH: AB^(→)|= AO^(→) + OB^(→); = − OA^(→) + OB^(→); = b − a; = (2i + 3j) − (− 2i + j); = 4i + 2j.]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Expressing Vectors as Differences of Position Vectors

Content:
If [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are points in the Cartesian plane with position vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] respectively, then

Content:
[MATH: \overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}.]

Content:
To understand why the equation above is true, remember that [MATH: \overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}.] Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: AB^(→)|= AO^(→) + OB^(→); = − OA^(→) + OB^(→); = − a + b; = b − a.]

Content:
For example, given [MATH: A(5,13)] and [MATH: B(-2,-35)], we have

Content:
[MATH: OA^(→) = a = 5i + 13j,; OB^(→) = b = − 2i − 35j.]

Content:
Now, using the formula, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: AB^(→)|= b − a; = (− 2i − 35j) − (5i + 13j); = − 7i − 48j.]
